posts.title: The Eight-Sided Pyramid
posts.hook: The Great Pyramid actually has eight sides
posts.narration: The Great Pyramid actually has eight sides. Each of its four main faces is slightly concave. This makes a very slight dip in the center. You can see this from the air. During the spring and autumn equinoxes, the sun hits the pyramid. The low sun puts half of a face in shadow. Follow us to learn more secrets.
posts.caption:
Did you know the Great Pyramid actually has eight sides?

It turns out each face is slightly curved inward. You can see this from the sky. A British Air Force pilot named P. Groves actually captured the first photo of it back in 1940. This is visible during the spring and autumn equinoxes when the low sun casts a shadow over half of a face. 😮

Do you think the builders did this on purpose or was it just an accident?

posts.fact: The Great Pyramid of Giza has eight sides due to its slightly concave faces, which are visible from the air during the spring and autumn equinoxes.

posts.title: Why Reindeer Eyes Turn Blue in Winter
posts.hook: Reindeer change their eye color every winter
posts.narration: Reindeer change their eye color every winter. In summer, their eyes are warm golden brown. When polar darkness hits, they turn deep blue, acting like built-in night vision. The constant dark increases pressure inside the eye, squeezing a tissue layer behind the retina to reflect blue light. That simple shift helps improve their vision in the dark. Follow along for more wild animal facts.
posts.caption:
I just found out reindeer change their eye color to see in the winter.

During the summer, a reindeer has golden brown eyes. But when winter brings constant polar darkness, pressure inside their eyes builds up. This extra pressure compresses a reflective tissue layer behind the retina, changing how light bounces off it and turning their eyes deep blue. Reflecting blue light helps improve their night vision in the dark.

Would you choose blue night vision if you had to live in total darkness? 🦌

#reindeer #arcticwildlife #reindeereyes #polarwinter #animaladaptations #aigenerated
posts.fact: Reindeer eyes change color from golden brown in the summer to deep blue in the winter to improve their vision in constant polar darkness.

posts.title: The Floating Paperclip
posts.hook: You can float a metal paperclip on plain tap water
posts.fact: A metal paperclip can float flat on the surface of plain tap water, supported by the water's surface tension.
posts.narration: You can float a metal paperclip on plain tap water. It sits there flat, looking like it is resting on a sheet of invisible plastic wrap. This works because cohesive hydrogen bonds between water molecules create a strong skin across the top. But if you disrupt that skin, it sinks. Hit follow for more.
posts.caption:
It is hard to believe this actually works.

It is wild to see a metal paperclip sit flat on top of plain tap water. It all comes down to hydrogen bonds. The water molecules hold onto each other to create a strong surface tension skin across the top. It is like a tiny, natural trampoline supporting the light metal object. One disruption and the tension breaks, sending the clip to the bottom. 🧪

Have you ever managed to get a paperclip to float on your first try?

posts.title: Squirrel Gravity Defiance
posts.hook: Gray squirrels can climb down trees headfirst safely
posts.fact: Gray squirrels can climb down trees headfirst because their hind ankles can rotate 180 degrees, allowing their claws to point backward and grip the bark.
posts.narration: Gray squirrels can climb down trees headfirst safely. It looks like they are defying gravity, running down a vertical trunk as easily as we stroll down a sidewalk. They can do this because their hind ankles can rotate 180 degrees. This lets their claws point backward to grip the bark. It is like wearing hiking boots backward. Follow for more.
posts.caption:
I just watched a gray squirrel climb headfirst down a tree and had to look up how they do it.

Turns out their hind ankles can rotate 180 degrees. This flexibility lets them point their claws backward, so they can grip the tree bark even when they're facing straight down. This allows them to run straight down safely. Honestly, it's wild how they move.

Have you ever seen a gray squirrel do this? 🐿️

posts.title: The Secret History of Bubble Wrap
posts.hook: Bubble wrap was actually invented to be wallpaper
posts.fact: Bubble wrap was invented in 1957 by Alfred Fielding and Marc Chavannes with the original intention of using it as textured wallpaper.
posts.narration: Bubble wrap was actually invented to be wallpaper. Back in 1957, two inventors sealed two plastic shower curtains together, trapping little pockets of air inside. They thought people would love having bumpy, textured walls in their living rooms, like living inside a giant cloud. But after that wallpaper idea failed, they marketed it as protective packaging instead. Hit follow for more weird history.
posts.caption:
I still can't believe bubble wrap was supposed to go on walls.

In 1957, Alfred Fielding and Marc Chavannes were trying to create a new home decor trend. They sealed two plastic shower curtains together, trapping air bubbles between them. When the whole wallpaper idea failed, they marketed it as protective packaging instead. It turns out that invention helped protect fragile items.

Would you ever cover your living room walls in bubble wrap?

posts.title: The Real Shape of Raindrops
posts.hook: Falling raindrops are shaped like tiny hamburger buns
posts.fact: Falling raindrops are shaped like flat-bottomed hamburger buns rather than teardrops because air pressure flattens their bottom as they fall.
posts.narration: Falling raindrops are shaped like tiny hamburger buns. We often draw them as perfect teardrops, but they are actually flat on the bottom and rounded on top. As they fall, the pressure of the air rushing past flattens the bottom. Meanwhile, surface tension keeps the top rounded. So, a storm is just millions of tiny hamburger-bun-shaped drops falling from the sky. Hit follow for more.
posts.caption:
I still can't believe we've been drawing raindrops wrong. Cartoons often show them as pointy teardrops, but actual physics says otherwise. When a drop falls, the pressure of the air rushing past flattens the bottom, while surface tension keeps the top rounded. It makes so much sense but it still feels weird to picture. Do you also feel a bit lied to by weather app icons?

#weather #science #raindrops #rainyday #storms #aigenerated
